exam: A 45‑year‑old man with hypertension presents with sudden unilateral facial weakness. Which imaging modality would you choose first and why? — Explain why MRA is preferred if contrast allergy is present.
You see a focal signal void on a brain TOF MRA. What does this indicate and what is your next step? — Identify possible aneurysm and recommend CTA or conventional angiography for confirmation.

A patient with renal failure needs evaluation for peripheral arterial disease. Which MRA technique is appropriate and what are its limitations? — Choose non‑contrast phase‑contrast MRA; note reduced spatial resolution.

During MRA of the abdomen, a double‑lumen sign is noted. What diagnosis does this suggest and how should management proceed? — Diagnose aortic dissection type B; start beta‑blocker and arrange serial imaging.
Explain how you would differentiate between true stenosis and artefact caused by a metallic implant on MRA. — Discuss artefact patterns and the role of alternative imaging.

A pregnant woman with suspected pulmonary embolism requires vascular imaging. What is the role of MRA? — State that MR pulmonary angiography avoids radiation and iodinated contrast, but may be limited by motion artefact.
What are the key contraindications to contrast‑enhanced MRA? — List severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 ml/min), gadolinium allergy, and certain metallic implants.
How does phase‑contrast MRA quantify flow, and why is this useful in peripheral arterial disease? — Describe velocity encoding and its correlation with stenosis severity.
ai.title: Magnetic Resonance Angiography
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: MRA uses magnetic resonance to visualise blood vessels without ionising radiation. It helps diagnose stenosis, aneurysm and dissection, especially when CT angiography is unavailable or contraindicated.

b: No ionising radiation – safe for young patients and repeated use
Time‑of‑flight (TOF) and phase‑contrast are common non‑contrast methods
sections.p: Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) is a non‑invasive imaging technique that exploits the magnetic properties of flowing blood to produce high‑resolution vascular maps. It can be performed with or without contrast agents.

b: Signal loss can occur with turbulent flow – may mask high‑grade stenosis
Metal implants cause artefact; assess compatibility before scanning
sections.p: MRA relies on differences in signal between stationary tissue and moving blood. In TOF sequences, unsaturated inflowing blood appears bright, while surrounding tissue is saturated and dark.

b: Detects intracranial aneurysms in sub‑arachnoid haemorrhage work‑up
Evaluates peripheral arterial disease when Doppler is equivocal
Assesses aortic dissection when CT is not feasible
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, MRA is valuable when CT angiography is unavailable, contrast is contraindicated, or radiation exposure must be minimised (e.g., pregnant women).

t.a: Non‑contrast TOF MRA of the brain
t.b: Is there an intracranial aneurysm or high‑grade stenosis? – Bright flow indicates patent vessels; absence or focal signal loss suggests occlusion or aneurysm sac
Is there an aortic dissection or renal artery stenosis? – Contrast fills true lumen; a double‑lumen sign indicates dissection; delayed enhancement suggests stenosis

t.a: Phase‑contrast MRA of the lower limbs
t.b: What is the quantitative flow velocity? – Reduced velocity points to severe peripheral arterial disease; normal flow excludes critical limb ischaemia
Is there significant arterial narrowing? – Elevated peak systolic velocity (>200 cm/s) correlates with >70 % stenosis

b: Aneurysm >7 mm or symptomatic – refer for endovascular coiling or surgical clipping
Critical limb ischaemia – antiplatelet (aspirin) plus risk‑factor control; consider revascularisation
Aortic dissection type B without complications – beta‑blocker to lower shear stress; monitor with repeat MRA
sections.p: Treat the underlying vascular pathology first; MRA guides choice of medical versus interventional therapy.

b: MRA vs. conventional angiography – conventional remains gold standard but is invasive and costly
sections.p: CT angiography (CTA) uses ionising radiation and iodinated contrast; it is faster but less suitable for renal impairment or pregnancy.

b: Always correlate with clinical picture and, if needed, alternative imaging
sections.p: Slow flow or turbulent jet can produce signal loss mimicking stenosis; artefacts from metal can obscure vessels.

b: Know when non‑contrast MRA is preferred (renal failure, contrast allergy)
Remember the ‘double‑lumen sign’ for aortic dissection on contrast MRA
sections.p: Focus on indications, advantages, limitations and interpretation pitfalls of MRA.
